prompt: rgb.jpg is a horizontal strip of 5 frames, left to right in time order, sampled from the few seconds of a head-mounted (egocentric) video; the camera wearer is the viewpoint. depth.jpg, segmentation.jpg and pose.jpg are the same 5 frames rendered as a monocular depth map (brighter = nearer to the camera wearer), an instance segmentation map (coloured masks with class labels), and a body/hand skeleton map (yellow = body, magenta = hands) on black. Look at all four images. For EACH of the three maps, describe the spatial understanding that map supports, using the RGB strip for context: the layout of the scene; which people and objects are present and roughly how far each is from the camera wearer (in metres) and from each other; relative positions (left/right/in front/behind, above/below); which way people face and whether they look toward the camera wearer; what is within arm's reach of the camera wearer or of others; occlusions and anything partly out of view; and how these change across the 5 frames (approach, retreat, turning). Say what each map shows that is hard to see in the RGB alone, and where the map looks unreliable. Describe only spatial facts. Do not guess anyone's intentions, social norms, or what anyone should do. Return only JSON: {"depth": "...", "segmentation": "...", "pose": "..."} with 3-5 sentences each.

descriptions.depth: Across the five downward-angled egocentric frames showing a carpeted room (~1.5–2.5 m to the upper walls) with no other people present, the depth map highlights the camera wearer's hands at the bottom center (~0.3–0.5 m away, within immediate arm's reach) and a black-and-white dog on the floor below (~1.0–1.5 m away) as brighter, nearer surfaces in frames 1, 2, and 5. In frame 1, the subtly brighter silhouette of the curved dog on the left (facing down toward the bottom center) helps distinguish its raised body volume from the flat floor plane, while frame 2 clearly separates the wearer's reaching hand at the bottom center and the dog beside it from the receding carpet and upper wall corner. In frame 5, the bright foreground contour at the bottom center accurately captures both of the camera wearer's hands brought together (~0.3–0.4 m away) above the floor as the dog moves nearly out of view at the bottom-right edge. However, the depth map is highly unreliable on the low-texture carpet as the camera turns and tilts across frames 3 and 4: frame 3 renders a false dark depression across the middle of the flat floor while missing the dog looking up at the bottom-right, and frame 4 hallucinates a massive bright foreground bulge on the empty lower-left floor while making the dog at the bottom-right appear darker and farther than the carpet behind it.
descriptions.segmentation: The instance segmentation map detects only two foreground regions across the entire five-frame sequence of the carpeted room and leaves the rest of the scene—including the walls (2.0–2.5 m at the top), the dark floor mat on the right (~1.5 m away in frames 1–3), and the chair on the left in frame 5—completely unsegmented. In frame 1, a tan mask cleanly delineates the full curved contour of the dog on the floor ~1.0–1.5 m below and to the left of the camera wearer (with its head angled down toward the bottom center), separating its dark fur from the shadowed carpet better than a quick glance at the RGB image. Across frames 2 to 5, the dog shifts from the bottom-left toward the bottom-right edge while orienting its head upward toward the camera wearer, and the wearer's hands enter at the bottom center (~0.3–0.5 m away, within arm's reach) in frames 2, 4, and 5. However, the map is largely unreliable in both classification and recall: it mislabels the dog in frame 1 as a bird ('birdr'), misclassifies the partially occluded dog at the bottom-right of frame 4 (~1.0–1.2 m away) as a 'person', and completely fails to segment either the dog in frames 2, 3, and 5 or the camera wearer's hands in any frame.
descriptions.pose: The body and hand skeleton map is entirely blank across all five frames, providing no spatial keypoints for the scene. In the RGB strip, no other people are present in the carpeted room—only a black-and-white dog on the floor ~1.0–1.5 m in front of and below the camera wearer that moves from the left in frame 1 across the bottom edge toward the bottom-right in frames 2–5, turning its head to look up toward the wearer in frames 2–4 while remaining partly cut off by the lower frame boundary. Because the camera is head-mounted and angled downward toward the floor (~1.5–2.0 m away) and upper walls (~2.0–2.5 m away), the camera wearer's torso is outside the field of view and no human body skeletons are expected. However, the pose map is unreliable for ego-hand tracking, as it completely misses the camera wearer's right hand reaching down near the dog at the bottom center of frame 2 (~0.4–0.5 m away), the fingertips at the bottom of frame 4, and both hands held together with fingers touching at the bottom center of frame 5 (~0.3–0.4 m away, well within arm's reach). Consequently, the map adds no information beyond the RGB frames and fails whenever the wearer's hands enter the lower boundary of the view.
